text: Days like this remind me why I love working with this team at Tidewater.  Six months ago we promised customers that alerts would arrive with a reason attached, not just a red number. Last night we turned that on for everyone. ✨  Every alert now says what changed, which service it touched first and which past incident it most resembles. Our own on-call engineers have been testing it since August, and the feedback that stuck with me came from Dev Ranganathan: “I went back to sleep because I could see it was the same disk problem as June.” That is exactly the outcome we were aiming for — fewer people woken up for things that can wait until morning.  A few numbers from the trial: Pages per engineer per week fell from eleven to four. Median time to the first useful note on an incident dropped from 19 minutes to 6. Not one of the alerts we suppressed turned out to matter.   Huge thanks to the people who made it happen: Ingrid, who argued for plain language in every message; Kofi, who rebuilt the event pipeline so the context arrives within seconds; and the twelve customer teams who let us watch their worst nights.  We also picked up the Southern Lights award for operations tooling along the way, which was a lovely surprise. 🏆  There’s plenty still to do. Next up is letting teams teach the system which changes they consider risky, and showing the reasoning behind every grouping. The plan is simple. Small and medium businesses get the same careful testing that large companies pay for, at a price they can plan around. Running a security team means choosing which risks to live with.   There is never enough time or budget to fix everything, so the real skill is deciding what waits — and explaining that choice to people who would rather not hear it.   On 20 November I’m joining a panel with Hana Oduya and Dev Ranganathan to talk about:  - How we rank findings when every scanner says critical  - What a useful risk register looks like after the audit is over  - When to push back on a deadline, and when to accept it  - How to keep a small team from burning out  - What we would tell our first-year selves   It’s free, it’s online, and there will be plenty of time for questions.   Register here: https://saltmarsh.example.org/panel-2026   Bring your hardest prioritisation story. We’ll bring ours, including the one we still argue about.  #CyberSecurity #CISO #RiskManagement #SecurityLeadership #InfoSec #Panel This Friday is a rest day at Tidewater, and the whole company is offline until Monday morning. We started doing this twice a year after a long run of launches, and it has become one of the things people mention most when they talk about working here. A few people asked how we manage it without leaving customers stranded, so here is the short version. Support runs a light rota, staffed by volunteers who take their own day off the following week. Every team writes a one-page handover on Thursday afternoon. The handover answers three questions: what could break, who to call if it does, and what can safely wait until Monday. Most are only a few lines long, and that is the point. No releases go out after Wednesday lunch. Managers are asked to set an example and actually log off, which is harder than it sounds. We track incidents across these weekends, and so far there have been fewer than on an ordinary Saturday, probably because nothing new ships. If you’re thinking of trying something similar, start with one day and a clear rule about releases. The rest follows. I wrote up our checklist and the email we send to customers beforehand: https://blog.example.com/rest-days​ And if you’d like to work somewhere that takes rest seriously, we’re hiring across engineering, design and support.
